newsitem.title: SWEDEN: December rush firms some ex-Sweden air cargo rates.
newsitem.headline: December rush firms some ex-Sweden air cargo rates.

text.p: Seasonal factors and a truckers' strike in neighbouring Denmark pushed air cargo traffic volumes from Sweden to higher levels, forwarders and airlines said.

The increase in turnover volumes typical in the pre-Christmas period was further boosted by the four-day strike, which forced some companies to send shipments by air which may have otherwise gone overland.

However, the Danish strike did not spark any increases in cargo rates because it was too short-lived, they said. Rates were instead steady -- a few slightly higher -- because of the usual holiday rush.

"Most airlines have implemented a surcharge in one form or another to cover additional costs and that's enough for the market to absorb," said Anders Uddman, British Airways cargo manager for northern Europe.
"On top of that, rates are not changed overnight," he said.
Kenneth Fernstrom, head of exports at freight forwarder Wilson, said the strike caused some congestion which had spilled over into surface transportation.
"Delays are expected, not rate increases. It's difficult to get space on ferries into Germany," he said before the Denmark dispute ended.
Finnair cargo spokesman Karl Berg said many charters were currently flying from Sweden. He attributed volume increases to seasonal factors.
"As far as I know there have been quite a lot of charters, especially to China," Berg told Reuters.
"As always, it's busier in December. The volume of mail, for example is increasing all over the world," he added.
Truckers blocked seaports and land borders in the industrial action, which ended last Thursday, forcing Scandinavian Airlines System to re-route some cargo through Paris and London airports.

Players said routes to the Far East, especially Hong Kong and China, were busiest. Sources said Ericsson recently chartered three Antonov-124 cargo planes to cope with telecoms shipments to the Phillipines.

"It's busier than last year because of the Swedish exports...namely because of the three biggest Ericsson companies -- radio, public telecoms and business, which produces telephone exchange switches," Singapore Airline's Jens Heide said.

"There's a lot of cargo going southwest to Argentina and Brazil, but also eastward, especially to China either directly or via Hong Kong, as well as to India," Sven Ahlberg, Lufthansa Cargo regional director Sweden, told Reuters.
Airlines and forwarders reported only minor rate changes besides the fuel surcharge of about 0.65 crown which was implemented by most airlines, albeit from different dates.
There was little protest about the fuel surcharge, which most say is simply a reality. "It's implemented, it's up and running," Ahlberg from Lufthansa said.
Denmark-based forwarders said their customers, who are generally smaller than their heavyweight Swedish export counterparts, were somewhat more resistant to the increase.
"In Sweden the shippers are bigger and seem to be prepared to pay," one forwarder said.

Rates to the United States were mixed. The average market rate to New York edged up to 9.90 crowns per kg from 9.75 one month ago for a 100 kg shipment, while to Chicago the rate was 11.25 crowns compared to 11.30.
The rate to Los Angeles was more or less stable, with the average rate at 12.75 crowns compared to 12.70 crowns.
One forwarder said airlines seemed to be able to take a shipment to the U.S. even at a moment's notice, although special rates below pre-agreed prices seemed to be the exception.
"Late on a Friday night we don't have any problems getting cargo onboard to the U.S., but to the Far East it would be impossible," one forwarder said.

Rates to the Far East were steady to higher. The rate to Hong Kong was flat at 13.30 crowns per kg while to Singapore it rose to 13.40 crowns from 13.30 at the time of the last market report. The rate to Bangkok was unchanged at 13 crowns.
To Tokyo the rate gained to 19.55 crowns from 19.40 crowns.
Swedish telecoms equipment, phamaceuticals, car spares and technical equipment were filling aircraft holds to Japan, market players said.

"The tendency is the price increases if you want space. Here in Sweden the prices are low, but if any agent wants space, he has to pay," said Berry Christensson, managing director of Swedish-based sales agents Air Consultants.
The average rate to Dubai was marginally lower at 10.20 crowns per kg compared to 10.25. To Johannesburg the rate rose slightly to 20.30 crowns from 20.10.
To London the rate averaged at 7.60 crowns compared to 7.50 crowns while to Paris the rate was steady at 7.30 crowns.
The rate to Sao Paulo was unchanged at 20.80 crowns. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
